lead: Wideband amplifiers keep gain flat over a large frequency range; tuned amplifiers do the opposite, giving high gain only around a chosen centre frequency. Wideband design fights the internal capacitances that cause the Miller effect. Tuned design uses an LC tank as the load and trades bandwidth for selectivity. These circuits appear in video drivers, oscilloscope front ends, radio receivers, TV tuners and mobile-phone RF front ends. The same transistor can be made wideband or narrowband by changing the load and the stage connection.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 for the Miller effect and Chapter 3.3 for the gain–bandwidth trade-off; Unit 2 for cascode and Darlington connections.

blocks.text: A wideband amplifier has a flat gain from its lower cut-off f<sub>L</sub> to its upper cut-off f<sub>H</sub>. Its figure of merit is the gain–bandwidth product (Chapter 3.3). To widen the band, keep the midband gain but stop the internal capacitances from forming a low-frequency pole. The main enemy is the Miller effect.

blocks.where: C<sub>M</sub> is the Miller capacitance at the input; C<sub>µ</sub> is the collector–base capacitance; A<sub>v</sub> is the voltage gain from base to collector. A large A<sub>v</sub> makes C<sub>M</sub> large and the input pole low.

blocks.text: The cascode connection uses a common-emitter (CE) transistor Q<sub>1</sub> followed by a common-base (CB) transistor Q<sub>2</sub>. The base of Q<sub>2</sub> is held at AC ground. Q<sub>2</sub> has a low input resistance, about 1/g<sub>m2</sub>, so the voltage gain of Q<sub>1</sub> is small, close to −g<sub>m1</sub>/g<sub>m2</sub> ≈ −1. The collector voltage of Q<sub>1</sub> therefore moves very little. Its Miller capacitance is about C<sub>µ</sub>(1+1)=2C<sub>µ</sub>, not C<sub>µ</sub>(1+|A<sub>v,total</sub>|). The overall voltage gain can still be high, about −g<sub>m1</sub>R<sub>L</sub>, because Q<sub>2</sub> passes the current to a high load resistance R<sub>L</sub>. Here g<sub>m</sub> is the transistor transconductance, and R<sub>L</sub> is the load resistance. The input pole moves up and the bandwidth increases. Cascodes appear in video drivers, oscilloscope front ends and RF low-noise amplifiers.

A common-collector (CC) stage followed by a CE stage is the CC-CE cascade. The CC stage is an emitter follower: its voltage gain is about 1, so its own Miller multiplication is small. It gives a high input resistance and a low output resistance, which drives the CE stage from a stiff source. The CE stage supplies the voltage gain. The CC-CE cascade is wider than a single CE stage because the input capacitance is isolated from the high-gain node. The FET version is the CD-CS cascade, with a common-drain stage driving a common-source stage.

A Darlington pair connects two transistors as CC-CC. The current gain is β<sub>1</sub>β<sub>2</sub>, and the input resistance is very high. As an emitter follower its voltage gain is slightly less than 1. It is used as a buffer before a wideband gain stage, not as the gain stage itself. A small capacitor C<sub>E</sub> across the emitter resistor R<sub>E</sub> gives emitter peaking. At low frequency C<sub>E</sub> is open and the gain is set by R<sub>E</sub>. At high frequency C<sub>E</sub> bypasses part of R<sub>E</sub>, raising the gain and compensating the high-frequency roll-off. Too much peaking causes overshoot.
A tuned amplifier uses an LC tank as its load. The tank stores energy at one frequency and rejects other frequencies. The centre frequency is where the reactances cancel.

blocks.where: f<sub>0</sub> is the centre frequency in hertz; L is the inductance in henry; C is the capacitance in farad.
Q is the quality factor, dimensionless; R is the series resistance of the coil in ohm; ω<sub>0</sub> = 2πf<sub>0</sub>.

blocks.text: For a coil with series resistance R, a high Q means low loss and a sharp resonance. The bandwidth is the band between the two 3 dB points:

blocks.where: BW is the 3 dB bandwidth in hertz; f<sub>0</sub> is the centre frequency in hertz; Q is the quality factor.

blocks.text: At resonance the tank looks like a resistance R<sub>p</sub> = L/(C R) = Qω<sub>0</sub>L = Q²R. A CE stage with transconductance g<sub>m</sub> has voltage gain |A<sub>v</sub>| = g<sub>m</sub>R<sub>p</sub> at resonance. Away from f<sub>0</sub> the impedance falls and the gain falls.

A single tuned amplifier has one LC tank. It is simple, but its passband is rounded and its skirts are not very steep. A double tuned amplifier couples two tanks. It gives a flatter top and steeper skirts, at the cost of more components and harder alignment. Some syllabi call the whole family an RF tuned amplifier. Tuned stages are used in radio IF amplifiers, TV tuners and as the load of class C stages (Chapter 3.7).

figure.caption: The tree separates wideband methods from tuned LC amplifiers. Notice that cascode, CC-CE and Darlington widen bandwidth, while single and double tuned circuits select a narrow band around the centre frequency.

spec.aria: A tree splits amplifiers into wideband techniques (cascode, CC-CE, Darlington) and tuned LC amplifiers (single and double tuned).

examples.question: A tuned amplifier uses a coil of L = 100 µH with series resistance R = 10 Ω, in parallel with C = 100 pF. Find the centre frequency f0 in MHz, the quality factor Q, and the 3 dB bandwidth in kHz.
steps: Convert units: L = 100×10<sup>−6</sup> H, C = 100×10<sup>−12</sup> F, R = 10 Ω.
examples.answer: The centre frequency is 1.591549 MHz, Q is 100.0, and the bandwidth is 15.91549 kHz.
examples.check:
import math
L = 100e-6
C = 100e-12
R = 10.0
f0 = 1.0/(2.0*math.pi*math.sqrt(L*C))
Q = (1.0/R)*math.sqrt(L/C)
BW = f0/Q
print(round(f0/1e6, 6))
print(round(Q, 1))
print(round(BW/1e3, 5))

traps: Q is not found from Q = f0/BW when the question gives L, C and R. First Q=(1/R)√(L/C); then BW=f0/Q.
Cascode does not remove Cµ; it reduces the voltage across it, so the Miller multiplication falls.
A tuned amplifier is narrowband, not wideband. Its high gain exists only near f0.
In f0, L must be in henry and C in farad: 100 µH = 100×10<sup>−6</sup> H and 100 pF = 100×10<sup>−12</sup> F.
Darlington pair gives high current gain and high input resistance, but voltage gain is slightly less than 1 when used as an emitter follower.

quiz.q: Define a wideband amplifier and a tuned amplifier in one line each.
quiz.a: A wideband amplifier has flat gain over a large frequency range. A tuned amplifier has high gain only near a chosen centre frequency set by an LC tank.

quiz.q: Why does the cascode connection reduce the Miller effect at the input?
quiz.a: The CB transistor loads the CE collector with a low resistance, so the CE stage voltage gain is about 1. The collector–base capacitance sees a small voltage swing, and C<sub>M</sub> is about 2C<sub>µ</sub> instead of C<sub>µ</sub>(1+|A<sub>v</sub>|).

quiz.q: A tuned amplifier has L = 200 µH, C = 50 pF and coil resistance R = 20 Ω. Find f0, Q and BW.
A CE stage has C<sub>µ</sub> = 2 pF and |A<sub>v</sub>| = 50. Find C<sub>M</sub>. If a cascode makes the first-stage gain 1, find the new C<sub>M</sub> and the ratio.
quiz.a: C<sub>M</sub> = 2 pF × (1+50) = 102 pF. Cascode: C<sub>M</sub> = 2 pF × (1+1) = 4 pF. Ratio = 102/4 = 25.5.

quiz.q: How does an emitter peaking capacitor extend the bandwidth?
quiz.a: At high frequency it bypasses part of the emitter resistor, so emitter degeneration falls and gain rises. This compensates the high-frequency roll-off. Too much capacitance causes overshoot.

quiz.q: A single tuned amplifier has f0 = 1 MHz and BW = 20 kHz. Find Q. If R is doubled, what happens to Q and BW?
quiz.a: Q = f0/BW = 1×10<sup>6</sup>/20×10<sup>3</sup> = 50. Q=(1/R)√(L/C), so doubling R halves Q to 25. BW=f0/Q then doubles to 40 kHz.

quiz.q: State two differences between single tuned and double tuned amplifiers.
quiz.a: Single tuned uses one LC tank; double tuned uses two coupled tanks. Double tuned gives a flatter passband and steeper skirts, but needs more components and harder alignment.

beyond: Not for the exam. In real RF chips, the cascode is the input stage of many low-noise amplifiers because it isolates the input matching network from the local oscillator. Tuned amplifiers appear in intermediate-frequency strips and in the load of class C power stages. Modern wideband design uses feedback and distributed amplifiers, which Unit 4 starts.
